newsitem.title: ISRAEL: An era ends for Peres in Israel's Labour party.
newsitem.headline: An era ends for Peres in Israel's Labour party.

text.p: Israel's Shimon Peres finally passed the torch to a new Labour Party generation after half a century in politics on Wednesday but vowed to go on working for Middle East peace.

The morning after former army chief Ehud Barak, 55, was elected to succeed him as party leader, a smiling Peres, 73, appeared relaxed and denied being sad about moving to the sidelines of Israeli politics.

"I wish I would be able also to resign from what I consider the most important effort in our history, namely the peace process. But this call cannot remain unanswered and I intend to continue," Peres said in an interview with Reuters.
"I think maybe in my new position I can do more than before because you know before everybody was calculating what sort of a job I'm looking for," he said. Now "I'm free from it."

Peres, who won the Nobel Prize in 1994 for making peace with Palestinians but lost time and again in Israeli elections, ventured he could do more for peace out of the spotlight and free of doubts about his political motives.

He vowed to go on speaking his mind in public, including in parliament where he has served for 38 years. He spoke with pride of a new peace institute named for him involving Tel Aviv and Harvard universities.
Peres said it would teach the art of negotiating peace while initiating projects by and for Israelis and Palestinians with the participation of European cities, the World Bank and businesspeople.

Israeli media have portrayed Peres and Barak as at odds with each other. But Peres said: "Undoubtedly he is an able man, he is an intelligent man, a man with experience and I do not see any reason why we can't work together."

Barak's rise barely two years into a political career marks a milestone for Labour. For 23 years the party was headed by the rival camps of Peres and Yitzhak Rabin, the prime minister assassinated in 1995 by a Jew opposed to their peace deals.

"I think he will learn," Peres said of Barak making peace. "He worked with us and he knows exactly that this was also the top issue in the eyes of Mr Rabin and myself and we are in the middle of the road. We cannot swim back."

Peres succeeded the slain Rabin as prime minister but lost the job a year ago to Benjamin Netanyahu following Palestinian Islamist suicide bombings that killed 59 people. Some Israelis blamed Peres for thinking he could make peace.

But asked if he felt unappreciated at times by his countrymen, Peres said: "You know I'm more afraid of adulation than of controversy. I think the minute I shall stop to be controversial, it will show that I stopped to dream and I stopped to look ahead and I stopped to introduce new ideas.
"So maybe controversy is the greatest of compliments if you want to move ahead," he said, adding that he believed that in the end most people agreed that his battle for peace was right.

Peres said he would not run for any other job now. He ruled out a unity government with Netanyahu's rightist Likud-led coalition, citing a corruption scandal dogging the Israeli leader. He assailed Netanyahu for a crisis in peacemaking.

"Netanyahu has had his chance. You judge a leader on his record and the year of the Netanyahu government is not a shining example of great achievements if at all. We have lost more than we have gained," Peres said.
"Peace is not singing a song. Peace is making very tough decisions -- costly, controversial -- and that is the test of a leader," he said.
